narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor, pushing the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was outweighed by two other features that pulled the outcome toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor. At 2.50, it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, and this lower performance increased the model's estimate of your risk of failing the bar. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the third strongest driver. Placing in the third decile, compared to an average around the sixth decile among accepted students, further raised the predicted probability of failure.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of not passing the bar was too high to offer admission.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score, improving your study habits to lift your GPA if you retake courses, and aiming for stronger class rankings in future semesters could meaningfully change future predictions. Consider speaking with an admissions counselor about additional ways to demonstrate your readiness before reapplying.
